Where Mom Keeps Everything

A one-page organizer for her statements, policies, deeds and tax returns: where each one is, how recent it is, and who has it.

Download PDF

The bank statements come in the mail and go in the kitchen drawer. The insurance policy is in a box in the closet, probably. The deed is “somewhere safe,” and the tax returns may be with whoever prepares them.

This page doesn't ask you to read or understand any of it. Go through it with Mom, and for each thing write where it is, how recent it is, and who has it.

What to collectWhere it isIts dateWho has it
Recent statements for checking and savings accounts, and any CDs
Recent statements for investment, brokerage and retirement accounts
Social Security and pension paperwork
Life insurance policies and annuity contracts
Long-term care insurance policy, if she has one
Health insurance cards and plan papers
Deed to her home, and records for any other real estate
Vehicle titles, and papers for any business interest or other significant property
Recent tax returns
Statements for any mortgage, loan or credit card

Scroll sideways to see every column, or print this page to fill it in.

What hasn't turned up yet, and who will look for it

Anything above with an empty line. Put a name next to each.

For example No copy of the life insurance policy. Mom will ask her agent for one the next time she calls.

Where the file will be kept, and who Mom wants to know

One secure place, chosen by Mom, and the name of anyone she'd like to know where it is.

For example Gray file box, bottom of the hall closet. Mom wants Denise to know. We'll look through it again in the spring.

How to use it

  • Write the date printed on each item. If it has no date, write “undated.”
  • Leave account numbers, Social Security numbers and passwords off this page. Just say where the paper is.
  • Don't rewrite or summarize a document here, and don't move one without Mom knowing where it went.
  • Put today's date on the page, and agree with Mom when you'll look at it again.

What this page doesn't do

It doesn't explain what any statement, policy or deed means, and it doesn't say which of them matter for Medicaid planning. If you read something you don't understand, that's a question for the company that issued it or for a professional. Nothing here is legal, financial or tax advice.
